subject: feat: word handles for terminals, shown as @moth (#181)
body:
## What

Terminals get a word handle such as `moth`, `fox` or `owl` instead of
`t1`, `t2`, `t11`. The handle shows as an `@moth` chip on every surface
that names a terminal, and agents write it the same way. What an agent
says now matches something on screen.

## Why

Agents talk about terminals by handle, but a person can't connect `t11`
to anything they see. The number appeared only inside the default title
"Terminal 11" and disappeared at the first rename. The counter also
never went down, so `t11` could be one of three open windows.

## Impact

- **Handles:** the words come from a ranked list, the Night Flock in
`runner/src/terminals/handles.ts`: night-sky and neon-street words plus
night birds.
- The list is checked against real agent transcripts so the words rarely
appear in agent output or code.
  - `handles.test.ts` enforces the list's rules.
- **Allocation:** each session gives a word once and never reuses it,
even after its terminal closes. A new `session_handles` table records
every word given.
- Only after every word is given does the list come round again as
`moth2`, `moth3` and so on.
- The next word prefers a first letter no open terminal in the session
has, then a word no other session has open.
- `terminals` gains `UNIQUE (session_id, handle)` and lists in the order
the handles were given.
- **UI:** `@moth` appears on window title bars in all views, on the
sidebar's second line, and in the switcher, search, notifications and
Messages. "led by @fox · name" uses it too.
- The close dialog and a companion's "From …" line name the terminal as
`@fox · name`, because default titles now repeat.
- Sidebar and notification rows announce the handle to screen readers as
their description.
  - Search finds a terminal by `fox` or `@fox`.
  - The demo uses words.
- **Agents:** tool answers and the agents listing write `@fox`, for
example `Opened a new terminal, @fox · codex, running codex in /work.`
Structured fields and XML attributes stay bare.
  - `send` and `close_terminal` accept `fox`, `@fox` or `@Fox`.
- The `agents` tool tells agents to name terminals to the person as
`@fox · title`.
- **Default title:** "Terminal 03" is gone. A terminal's default title
is the program it was opened to run, else `Terminal`.
- **Voice:** dictation adds the session's open handles to the whisper
hint, so it spells them right.
- **Not done yet:**
- The demo and UI fixtures still name new terminals "Terminal NN", which
their specs rely on.

subject: feat: open agent plans beside the terminal and edit them there (#188)
body:
## What

Agent plans open in the companion pane on their own and can be edited
there, with inline notes working. Finished deliverables an agent shows
open too.

- A plan observed live opens when it is first created (its event is
under 60 s old). Later rewrites while the agent drafts only refresh it,
marked new; replays after a restart stay closed.
- New `companions.save({ itemId, text, basedOn })` writes a plan kept in
a file: temp file, fsync, rename over it (symlinks followed, mode kept),
refused with the plan as it now stands when its stamp changed, checked
again just before the rename, and serialized per item. Plan content now
carries `writable` and `skill`, which the UI adapter passes through
instead of hardcoding both false.
- Plans in an agent's transcript, and plans over 256 KiB, stay
read-only; the pane says why.
- The `show` description and the artifacts notice now tell agents to
pass `open` for a finished deliverable and leave it off for supporting
files.

## Why

Plans never opened by themselves, and the editor and its notes were
there but unreachable: the adapter marked every plan read-only and
`save` rejected. Other artifacts had stopped opening because #130 told
agents to show finished work quietly and `open` only when asked, which
its description doesn't record as a decision.

## Impact

- `skill` comes from `agents.connected` in the router, so it refreshes
on the next content change, not the moment the plugin is connected.
- A save replaces the file, so hard links to a plan keep the old text.
- A save that can never succeed (file deleted) still retries; a stacked
follow-up handles it.
- A plan the person closes stays closed until the runner restarts (the
dismissal is in memory); only a root agent's plan opens the pane, not a
subagent's.
- Unreproduced: if the UI lags or reconnects, `companions.watch` can
coalesce a plan's first and second version, so the UI sees only version
2 (`asked: false`) and the plan never auto-opens.
- An `agents.connected` failure would surface as a raw error from
`save`/`content`; today's harnesses catch their own.
- Running agent sessions hear the new `open` wording at their next
session start or compaction.
- The demo backend still can't show the read-only state.

Checks: build, format, lint, typecheck and tests pass. A browser test
(`opens a plan's editor as it was left`) failed once under full-suite
load and passed in isolation and on rerun. Not run in the live app.

subject: feat: answer agents from the Inbox in the real app, on the runner (#195)
body:
## What

The Inbox now works in the real app. Until now it ran only on the demo
backend. On the runner it replaces the Notifications panel and the bell,
on by default, and you answer each row where it is:

- **Approve/Ask:** permission, plan and question dialogs from every
project, answered through `agents.answer`. A dialog Novadeck can't read
opens an "answer it in the terminal" sheet.
- **Held messages:** an agent-to-agent thread held for going back and
forth too often. You can Release it or, new here, **Stop** it
(`messages.stop`).
- **Trouble:** a failed turn with its error, where you can ask the agent
to fix it. A usage limit with its window and reset time, where you can
Continue once it has reset.
- **Updates:** a finished turn with its reply (or murmur's gist) and the
files it wrote. These clear when you read them or open the terminal.

You get one row per agent, the most urgent first. A pending request
beats an older finish. Held threads always show.

## Why

The site promises you won't have to babysit agents. The Inbox is how
Novadeck keeps that: you see what each agent is waiting on and answer it
from one queue, without watching terminals. It also backs the hero's
"pings you" copy, starting in-app.

## Impact

- **Runner and protocol:**
  - `lastTurn` gains `error`, `limit` and `files`.
  - Requests gain `askedAt`.
  - Threads gain `stopped`, and there is a new `messages.stop`.
- Stopping a thread drops its waiting messages, including leased ones
whose lease lapses.
    - The senders are told once.
- Sends between the pair are refused for 10 minutes from the later of
the stop and the last message.
- A limit is latched only on the harness's own signal (Claude
`rate_limit`, Codex `usage_limit_exceeded`, Antigravity
`RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`). Telemetry within 60 s of the turn's end only
supplies the reset time.
- **Harnesses (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity):**
- All three decoders now carry a failed turn's error and the limit
signal.
- Antigravity's `replace_file_content` is now decoded as a file the
agent wrote, and its "Accept this file edit?" prompt can now be
answered.
  - Codex patches run through its shell are read from the rollout.
  - Only writes that succeeded count as files.
- **Answering (found by CI, where Codex's sandbox fails and it asks
about each edit):**
- Confirming an answer now re-reads the other pending requests while it
waits, because Codex raises its next permission only as that prompt
appears. Before this, a correct answer to a

subject: feat(ui): assistive technology hears who leads whom in a team's tab descriptions (#330)
body:
## What

Each team member's sidebar tab now names its team in its accessible
description, with nothing added on screen. A worker says "led by @moth",
a lead says "leads @fox and @owl", and a terminal that does both says
both. A big team names the first three workers by handle, then counts
the rest.

## Why

Follow-up to #328. The rail's team wire is only drawn and is hidden from
assistive tech, so a screen reader had nothing but a worker's "led by"
in its window header. Nothing said which terminals a lead leads.

## Impact

- **When it's said:** the words are there whatever is selected, unlike
the wire, because the selection-time drawing is no help to someone who
can't see it.
- **Where it's said:** it uses the description channel the tab already
has, a hidden span named by `aria-describedby`.
- **Tests:** core tests cover the wording, and a behaviour spec covers
the descriptions. Existing spec assertions on the messages demo's lead
and worker descriptions now include their team.

subject: feat(ui): the sidebar shows the selected terminal's team on the rail's border (#328)
body:
## What

While the selected terminal leads others, or works for a lead that runs,
the Terminals sidebar shows its team. The border between the icon rail
and the sidebar lights up from the team's topmost tab to its bottommost.
A block cursor marks the lead, and a tick reaches each worker's tab.
Selecting a member sends one pulse out from the lead along the wire. The
team's other tabs take a faint accent tint, and their handles light up,
with the lead's in a chip.

## Why

When an agent opens terminals with a brief, it leads them. Until now
only the worker's window header said so ("led by @moth"), so the sidebar
couldn't show who leads whom at a glance. The design was settled over
several sketch rounds on a frozen copy of the app:

- Tabs never say it in words and show nothing at rest.
- The relation shows only while one of the team is selected, with no
hover preview.
- The selected tab keeps its accent bar and is never tinted.
- Out of view, the wire runs into the list's edge.

## Impact

- **Team rule:** the team follows the same running-lead rule as the
header's "led by". A terminal that both works for a lead and leads
others shows the team it leads.
- **Drawing:** the wire is an overlay in the workspace body, because the
sidebar clips anything drawn outside it. It measures the rail and the
tabs, and follows scrolling, resizes, tab changes, drag reorders and the
drawer/desktop swap. The Terminals list announces its element through a
small store the workspace provides.
- **Phone width:** the drawer shows the tint but no wire, since there's
no desktop rail to light.
- **Demo:** the debug panel gains "Leads the others". With "Burst of"
first, you can reach large teams and members scrolled out of view.
- **Tests:** unit tests cover the team derivation and the wire geometry,
and behaviour specs cover selecting the lead, a worker, an unrelated
terminal, and the lead closing. One more spec checks that clicking away
doesn't leave the old wire drawn.

subject: refactor(runner): terminals' saving moves out of manager.ts into a Saves module (#329)
body:
## What

Step 1 of splitting `backend/runner/src/terminals/manager.ts` (design:
`architecture/manager-split.md` in the workspace). Persistence moves out
of the `Terminals` class
into `terminals/saving.ts`, behaviour unchanged:

- **`Saves`** holds every read and write of the terminal records. It has
`persisting` (each with
the same `until` as before), `save`, `saved` and `identity`, the
periodic saver (`start`,
`stop` and the private `persistSome`), `persist`, and `keep`
(transcripts on or off). It also
has the guarded reads and writes the manager used to inline:
`terminals`, `giveHandle`,
`rename`, `clearMurmurTitles`, `forgetAgent` and `remove`. Its host is
three lazy callbacks:
  `stopping`, `stopped` and `records`.
- **`record.ts`** holds the `Record` and `Started` types, moved
verbatim, so later modules can
  name the slice of a record they touch.
- **Pure functions:** a saved terminal's summary (`savedSummaryOf`, in
`summary.ts`) and a
  summary's title (`summaryTitle`, in `naming.ts`).
- **`e2e/trace.ts`** wraps `Saves.prototype.persisting` instead of the
manager's, and now
passes `until` on. Before, a traced run dropped it, so `saved()` and the
removal in
`forget` ran as "untilStopping" while tracing. This affects only e2e
tracing.
- `manager.test.ts`'s two "saving a terminal that was closed" cases now
reach `saves.save`.
- `scripts/ratchet/manager.json` comes down to the new counts.

Where it went, for a branch that touched these methods:

| Was on `Terminals` | Now |
|---|---|
| `persisting`, `save`, `saved`, `identity` | `this.saves.persisting`,
`.save`, `.saved`, `.identity` |
| `persistSome`, `saveChanges`, `saver` | `Saves` (private),
`this.saves.start()` and `.stop()` |
| `transcripts` | `this.saves.transcripts` |
| `keepTranscripts`, `persist` | stay public, now one-line delegates |
| `savedSummary`, `titled` | `savedSummaryOf` (`summary.ts`),
`summaryTitle` (`naming.ts`) |
| `type Record`, `type Started` | `terminals/record.ts` |

## Why

`manager.ts` is the agent layer's ~4.3k-line hub, with about 160 methods
over one mutable
record per terminal. This is the first of ten behaviour-identical steps
that move each concern
behind a narrow host, as `ringing.ts` does for the doorbell. Persistence
goes first because
every other concern calls it.

## Impact

None for users: a refactor. `manager.ts` goes from 4,348 to 4,054 lines
and from 163 to 155
methods, and the ratchet is lowered to match.

Checks on the head:
- `format:check`, `lint` and `ty

subject: fix(scripts): move-frontend's settled forms are fragments that outlive later flags, and 5.3c's forms of its lines count as made (#324)
body:
## What

`node scripts/packages/move-frontend.ts`, 5.3b's script, has nothing to
do on main again. After
5.3c (#321) it stopped instead: "application/host/electron-builder.yml
is gone (a path from the
host, one folder deeper): the edit needs a new place".

- **The host edit is read where 5.3c moved the host.**
- `move.ts`'s `Edit` gains `later`, the file's place after a later
step's move.
  - Once the file is gone from its old place, the edit reads it there.
- Its `settled` form is the line that move wrote:
`electron-builder.yml`'s `- from: dist`.
- **The UI's `vite.config.ts` isn't made again.**
- The script writes it from a template wherever it's missing, and 5.3c
deleted it.
  - Past the stop, a run would have brought it back.
- Its `made` entry gains `until: "apps/desktop/vite.config.ts"`, the
file that took its place.
- **The lines 5.3c and #317 changed count as made, so the run lists
nothing.**
  - `settled` matches by substring.
- So the three root test lines' forms (138f93c8) are now the fragments
that mark the split by
package. They outlive a later flag such as #317's
`--output-logs=new-only`, which brought
    the "nothing to do" notes back.
- The four edits whose lines 5.3c rewrote take 5.3c's forms: the browser
fence's files,
    `libraries/README.md`, and two README passages.
- **A new test, `frontend.tree.test.ts`**, runs the plan over the
repository itself, and expects
  no problem, no move, no removal and no write.

## Why

The 5.3b catch-up recipe in `scripts/packages/README.md` ends with a run
that should say
"Nothing to do". After #321, that run stopped on every branch that
merged main. @owl found it
while reviewing 5.4 (#323, S1).

## Impact

- **On main,** the script prints "Nothing to do" alone, and exits 0.
- **The new test** fails without the fix, on the stop. With only the
host edit fixed, it fails on
  the remade `frontend/ui/vite.config.ts`.
- **On #323's tree (241e8292),** the plan makes no move and no write.
- Its only problems are two edits to `scripts/core/README.md`, which
#323 deletes along with
    those edits.
- It lists six edits whose lines #323 rewrites. That's why the test
doesn't assert the list is
    empty, so the two PRs merge in either order.
- **Local checks, under `env -i`:** format, lint, typecheck and
`test:repository` (32 files, 550
  passed, 4 skipped).
- **CI:** the usual checks. The new test reads every tracked file, so it
gets a minute, as the
  git tests do.

subject: fix(harnesses): Codex 0.163's prompt shown as a tail and its steered prompts are read (#305)
body:
## What

The nightly e2e against the latest Codex (0.163.0) passes again: two
things changed on Codex's screen, and the deck now reads both.

- **A prompt taller than Codex's box shows only its tail.**
- From 0.163.0, Codex draws a text taller than its box in a box of a set
height: floor(2 × (rows − 6) / 3) rows, which is 12, 16, 22 and 29 rows
on screens of 24, 30, 40 and 50 rows. Only the text's last lines show,
with a dim `↑` at the end of the box's first row.
  - Up to 0.160.1 the box grew to `room` and showed the whole text.
- `harnesses/codex/src/box.ts` gains a `viewport`, the box's height on a
screen of a given height.
- A shared `showsTail` in `libraries/tui-input/src/box.ts` says when a
box shows the tail of a text: it fills the viewport, and the text ends
with what it shows. Two checks use it:
    - the interrupt check, to tell that a prompt was put back;
- the paste check (`Prompts.landed`), to tell that a prompt landed
before it sends Enter.
- A box shorter than its viewport still has to show the whole text, so a
short box showing only the end of a text is never taken for it.
- **Codex steers a prompt given mid-turn into the running turn.**
- 0.163.0 adds it to the running turn's model call at once, so that
call's one reply answers both prompts.
- Where the harness steers, the fake model's rule in chat.e2e's "queues
a prompt given mid-turn…" now gives that reply. That matches how the
case already treats the queued pair.
- **On macOS, Codex 0.163.0 draws ctrl as `⌃`:** "Side from main thread
· ⌃/ to switch · ⌃c to close".
- The Codex harness's `overlay` took only `ctrl+` and `^`. On a Mac it
would miss a `/side` conversation, and read the side's box as the
root's.
  - It now takes `⌃` too, as does codex.e2e's `side`.
- The approval dialogs' shortcut reader also reads `^x` and `⌃x` as
ctrl.
- **A recorded screen for 0.163.0:** the input-box probe records a
40-line text at 24, 30, 50 and 40 rows. `fixtures/input-box.probe.json`
gains a `0.163.0` entry, which box.test reads, along with the box's
height at each screen height.

## Why

Since 10-16, the nightly e2e has failed on Codex on all three systems.
It runs the latest Codex, not the pin. Two cases failed:

- **chat.e2e, "queues a prompt given mid-turn as the person's would be,
and answers both":** the fake model never answered the second prompt,
because Codex had already given it to the first call.
- **interrupt.e2e, "clears a long prompt put back in the box, though it
shows only its tail, and

subject: feat(demo): the try demo's terminals are real terminal output, drawn by the app's own terminal views (#285)
body:
## What

Step 3's 3.2d: the demo's terminals are real terminals, drawn the way
the runner's are.

- **One rendering path.**
- The demo backend mounts its terminals through
`@novadeck/terminal/view`'s `createTerminalViews` and the shared
`createTerminalMount`, as the runner does.
- It offers `mountTerminal`, `setFont` and `typeInto` in place of its
React `TerminalSurface`. The port's `TerminalSurface` variant stays for
3.2c to remove.
  - The demo is a stream source (`backend/demo/views.ts`):
- on attach it writes a snapshot of the whole screen, then output as
things change;
    - keys come back through `write`;
    - `resize` draws the screen again at the new width.
- Lock, resume, parking, the WebGL pool, retheme, paste, `typeInto`,
search and the input's name ("Input for …") all come from the views.
- **The views' glue is shared.**
- `backend/terminal-views/` holds the mount, theme, renderers, links,
platform, the emulator opener, the paste notice's words and the screen
styles (`terminal-xterm.css`, class `.terminal-xterm`), moved out of
`backend/runner/`.
- It imports only the core, the port and libraries, and only backends
and tests import it. The architecture test checks both.
- The page's theme comes in as the port's `ThemeSource`, built by the
entries from `theme/probe` and `theme/apply`. It's passed through
`connectRunnerBackend(signal, progress, { transport, theme })`, the
visitor's and the preview's connects, and the spec backend. No backend
imports `theme/` any more, and `RunnerBackendOptions.theme` is required.
- **What the demo writes (`backend/demo/screen/`).**
  - **The screen model is pure:**
- an append-only transcript: the program's sample output or the agent's
opening, the commands typed and their replies, and the agent's
conversation;
- a live tail redrawn in place: the dialog the agent waits on in a box,
the note, the status lines, and the prompt between two rules.
  - **How the tail redraws:**
    - It moves up to its first row and erases below.
- When it keeps its height, only the rows that changed are written. A
row that only grew writes what it gained, and one that only shrank is
erased from there.
- A resize, a rerun or a tail taller than the screen draws everything
again.
  - **How text is laid out:**
    - styles come from the theme's ANSI palette;
    - words wrap at the column count;
    - widths and graphemes are counted as the emulator counts them.
- **Each terminal's writer** (`screen/terminal.ts`) outlives the
streams. It

subject: feat(wire): server sessions, the gate and the handshake, in the wire library (#253)
body:
## What

Step 2's W4: the runner's server side of the connection moves into
`@novadeck/wire/server`, and the handshake into the wire. It stacks on
W5 (#238) for the `./server` subpath.

- **`createSessions({ protocolVersion, router, admit, closed, error,
epoch })`** holds what `router.ts`'s `Connection` and `runner.ts`'s
`connect`/`disconnect`/`claim` held:
- each session's id, client id, whether it authenticated or closed, and
its calls in flight;
  - the epoch, which names the server's lifetime;
- takeover: a client's new session closes its older one and ends that
one's transport.

`closed(session)` tells the app a session ended. The runner releases
terminal control, voice and murmur there, as `disconnect` did.
- **The handshake is the wire's own.** `wireContract` is `{ wire: {
handshake } }`, and the protocol spreads it into its contract in place
of `runner.handshake`.
- The handshake takes `{ protocolVersion, token?, clientId? }` as before
and answers `{ epoch, protocolVersion }` (it was `runnerId`).
- `createSessions` serves it: `UNAUTHORIZED` for a bad token,
`INCOMPATIBLE_PROTOCOL` for another version, then the app's `admit`,
which may refuse with a code of its own.
- The refusing runner is now an `admit` that throws `WORKSPACE_TOO_NEW`,
and `refusal.ts` is gone.
- `connect()` drops its `handshake` option for `protocolVersion`. It
calls the wire's handshake itself and refuses a server that answers
another version.
- **The gate** sits in front of every procedure of the app's router:
- a session that hasn't authenticated, or has closed, is `UNAUTHORIZED`;
  - past `maxCalls` calls, a call is `RESOURCE_LIMIT`;
- failures go through the app's `error` mapping (the runner's
`apiError`), its codes beside the wire's.

A stream a procedure returns is guarded too: it ends once its session
closes, even one that closed before the stream began, and its failures
are mapped the same way. That replaces nine `if (closed) return; try {
yield* … } catch { throw apiError(…) }` copies in `router.ts`, plus
`attach`'s try/catch and `asks.watch`'s check per item. Each stream
handler now just hands its service's stream back, except
`companions.content`, which still adds each plan's plugin state.
- **`serveWebSocket(sessions, options)`** replaces
`runner/src/websocket.ts`. It takes as options what it read from the
runner or hard-coded: `path`, `maxPayloadBytes`, `sendBudgetBytes`,
`maxCalls` (32), `authMs` (10 s), plus `maxConnections` (32),
`heartbeatMs` (30 s), `origins`,

subject: feat(addons): offer voice input and murmur in context, one click each (#203)
body:
## What

Voice input and Murmur are now offered in the place where each one
helps. Turning either on takes one click, and nothing downloads until
that click.

- **Voice input.** The mic button and Ctrl+Shift+M are always available.
The first time someone uses either one, the dictation strip at the foot
of the terminal (the bar that shows Listening and Transcribing) offers
voice input, with No thanks and Turn on.
- That same strip then shows the download and "Voice input is ready.
Hold Ctrl Shift M to talk.", and any failure with a Try again.
- Pressing the chord again, or clicking the mic, also means Turn on. Esc
stays with the agent. Ignoring the offer only dismisses it.
- No thanks hides the mic and passes the chord through to the terminal.
- While setup is showing, the strip takes its own row, so the agent's
input stays visible. If the terminal is off screen, the strip's states
show in the pill at the foot of the app.
- **Voice model.** It installs turbo, then quietly falls back to small
when turbo is unfit for this computer. People no longer pick a model.
- **Murmur.** After an agent finishes its first turn, a quiet "Name it
for me" chip appears next to that terminal's plain title, opening a
popover. It only shows on a terminal that is on screen.
- No thanks declines for good. An unanswered chip comes back in at most
three sessions.
- The download shows as a footer item with a sheet, the same way updates
do.
- **Wording.** The word "GPU" never appears. A computer that can't run
Murmur shows "Not available on this computer", with the reason under
Details and a Check again.

## Why

Without these addons, people miss part of Novadeck. A 2 GB download on
first launch would break the calm, so each addon is offered at the
moment its value shows. In a pilot, someone read "Needs a GPU" as
needing a discrete card. The layout was chosen from a mockup of several
options: nothing floats over terminals.

## Impact

- **"Not available" is kept only for real incompatibility.** That
verdict is tied to the engine build. Timeouts, running out of memory
(for example when the person's own Ollama is holding the video memory)
and crashes stay retryable.
- **Software-only rendering check (Windows only).** The host reports it
with `--novadeck-graphics=software`. Linux and macOS skip the check,
because Electron's `getGPUInfo` there only enumerates PCI devices and
can exit the app when `/sys/bus/pci` can't be read.
- **Protocol.** `murmurState` gains `unsupported: {reason, sour

subject: feat(inbox): add agent ask and tell tools (#198)
body:
## What

Add MCP `ask` and `tell` tools for Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity.
Agents can ask through the Inbox and continue working; the person's
answer arrives later as authenticated mail. Questions, updates and
replies remain in Messages under **You**.

## Why

The runner-backed Inbox could display native dialogs and agent status,
but agents could not produce its Ask or Told items. This connects those
existing sheets to real agent tools and reply delivery.

## Impact

Asks support free text, up to three options and actions for the person
to complete. They clear when answered, withdrawn or their agent session
ends. Told updates remain until read while their terminal exists and do
not badge the bell. Secret requests are omitted; Novadeck does not write
secrets to project files or execute action instructions.

Replies are bound to the asking session, saved atomically with the
resolved ask and delivered through the existing mailbox. Only the
authenticated UI API can create a person-attributed reply. Person
replies bypass the agent-to-agent messaging pause and use a separate
bounded queue. Agent-written questions and labels are quoted separately
from the person’s own answer. The pre-release workspace schema changes
without a migration, following the existing database reset policy.

Creation is rate-limited, ask and tell capacities are separate, and
resolved history is capped and expires. Messages distinguishes withdrawn
asks, ended sessions and undelivered replies. Reply fields enforce 4,096
characters and preserve drafts on errors.

Validation: repository formatting, lint, typechecking and tests; options
and action Inbox scenarios on Claude Code, Codex and Antigravity,
including the actual schemas those harnesses expose to the model;
independent reply-authority/lifetime review; and an interactive demo
check of Ask → reply → Messages history.

subject: feat(chat): chat view for agent terminals, read from their own transcripts (#100)
body:
## What

Agent terminals (Claude Code, Codex, Antigravity) get a **Chat** view: a
toggle in the window header that renders the agent's own conversation
like a chat app, read live from its session transcript (no `claude -p`
or second agent process), with a composer that types prompts into the
real TUI and a Stop button.

## Why

Agents running in a terminal are hard to follow as a conversation: long
tool output scrolls replies away, and there's no readable history. The
runner already parsed every harness's transcript (`agents.transcript`,
`agents.detail`); nothing rendered it. This puts a chat on top of the
same running session instead of replacing it, so hooks, resume, plugins
and messaging keep working.

## Impact

- **UI** (`terminals/chat/`, `model/conversation*.ts`): your messages as
bubbles; agent replies as rendered markdown with highlighted code; tool
calls summarised in one line per tool (Bash/Read/Edit/Grep/Task…, Codex
`exec_command`/`apply_patch`/`update_plan`, Antigravity
`run_command`/`view_file`/…), expandable to input and result; messages
from other agents; working/planning/subagent status; pending
permission/question/plan requests as cards with **Answer in terminal**.
Stick-to-bottom scrolling, a window of recent blocks with "show
earlier". The terminal stays mounted at full size underneath (inert
while chat shows), so switching back is instant and lossless. Mode and
draft are per terminal, kept through runner hiccups, dropped when the
agent ends; not persisted across reloads.
- **Port**: optional `backend.conversations` (`conversation(key)`,
`send`, `interrupt`), implemented by the runner adapter (follows
`agents.detail` + `agents.transcript`, lazy with a 30 s grace, no
flicker on reconnect) and the demo (`?demo=agents` has a conversation
for each agent).
- **Runner/protocol**: new `agents.prompt` (pastes the text as one
bracketed paste with the person's keys held, checks it landed in the
agent's box, then presses Enter; `PROMPT_FAILED` leaves it as a draft)
and `agents.interrupt` (Escape; clears the prompt Claude Code restores
to its box so it isn't sent twice). Both go through the same bookkeeping
as the person's keys (naming, typed-prompt attribution, `turn-escaped`,
messaging states). Mid-turn prompts behave as typed ones: Claude Code
and Antigravity queue them, Codex injects after the next tool call.
- **Tests**: unit tests per module; behaviour spec
`specs/chat.spec.tsx`; e2e `runner/src/e2e/chat.e2e.ts` on the real
Claude Code, Code

subject: perf(ui): off-screen Canvas nodes release their screens and stop laying out (#261)
body:
## What

Canvas nodes out of sight stop streaming and stop laying out. This is
the Canvas half of
performance rule 13.

- **Canvas watches its nodes.** One IntersectionObserver
(`layouts/canvas/nodeVisibility.ts`)
is rooted at React Flow's `.react-flow`, the element that clips the
nodes. Its margin is about
one node (400 px vertically, 550 px horizontally), so a node coming in
from the edge has its
  screen back before it shows. Each node gets an on-screen flag.
- **Surfaces learn on-screen.** `TerminalSurfaceProps`
(`backend/port.ts`) gains an optional
`onScreen?: boolean`, true by default, so Focus, Grid and the demo
surface are unchanged. The
Canvas node sets it, and it reaches the surface through
`TerminalLayoutControls`
  (`terminals/WindowShell.tsx`) and `WorkspaceTerminal`.
- **The runner surface lets its screen go while off screen.**
`RunnerTerminal` acquires its
screen while `onScreen` holds and releases it when it goes false,
staying mounted. The screen
parks after 5 s and counts toward the parked-screen cap of 16. Back on
screen, the surface takes
the screen again, and it resyncs from the runner's snapshot. Every
acquire pairs with one
release, an unmount while off screen included. A surface sets `refocus`
only on a real unmount.
- **The node hides.** 6 s after a node leaves sight, so after its screen
has parked, its content
gets `content-visibility: hidden` (never `auto`; see the rule). The hide
comes off in the same
render that sees the node back, before the surface takes its screen, so
xterm measures a
  laid-out element.
- **A node that has never been on screen opens no screen** until it's
panned in.
- **Focus waits for the node.** `WorkspaceTerminal` gives a surface
keyboard focus only while it's
on screen. A jump to a node panned away waits until it's back, rather
than focusing a hidden
textarea and losing the request. A request stands until the focus lands,
so a node whose screen the parked-screen
  cap closed while it was away still takes it when it opens again.
- **Tests:**
- A new `canvas-offscreen.spec.tsx` (behaviour project, scripted runner,
real timers) covers:
    - a node far off screen at first load opens nothing;
- a node just past the edge, within the margin, opens its screen and
isn't hidden;
- panning a node out parks it and hides it, never while its screen is
still open, and panning
      it back un-hides it, attaches again and shows what it missed;
    - focus sent to a hidden node lands in its input once it's back.

subject: fix(ui): the app's shortcuts work from a terminal, ahead of its emulator (#282)
body:
## What

The app's shortcuts work again when typed into a terminal:
- the terminal switcher (Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+Shift+Tab);
- the Focus toggle (Ctrl+Shift+Enter, ⌘Enter on a Mac);
- Find, Preferences, a new terminal, session or Zen;
- Escape and Enter while the switcher is open.

From terminal input (but not a chat's box), the keymap's `switcher`,
`anywhere` and `app` layers now run in the capture phase, ahead of the
terminal's emulator, as the jumps already do. Elsewhere they still run
in bubble, as before.

## Why

A runner terminal's emulator (xterm) reads the keys it handles and
cancels them before they bubble: Ctrl+Tab becomes a Tab,
Ctrl+Shift+Enter becomes Enter, and Escape goes to the program. Those
layers ran in bubble, so in the desktop and web apps these shortcuts
never ran from a terminal. They went to the shell instead.

`interaction/shortcuts.ts` says modifier shortcuts "also work from
terminal input". The specs never caught this, because they ran on the
demo, whose terminals were a plain `<input>` until 3.2d.

## Impact

- **Every chord now taken from a terminal, and what the terminal gave it
before.** The three layers hold only these. The source is
`interaction/shortcuts.ts`; what xterm sent comes from xterm 6's
`evaluateKeyboardEvent`.

| Chord (Linux, Windows · Mac) | App command | xterm before | Changes
for a shell? |
  |---|---|---|---|
| Ctrl+Tab · Ctrl+Tab | Recent terminals | Tab (`\t`), cancelled | yes:
no longer a Tab; plain Tab still completes |
| Ctrl+Shift+Tab · Ctrl+Shift+Tab | Previous recent terminal | back-tab
(`ESC[Z`), cancelled | yes: plain Shift+Tab still sends back-tab |
| Ctrl+Shift+Enter · ⌘Enter | Toggle Focus view | CR, cancelled | yes:
plain Enter is untouched |
| Ctrl+Shift+K · ⌘K | Find a terminal | nothing | no: it reached the app
already |
  | Ctrl+Shift+T · ⌘T | New terminal | nothing | no |
  | Ctrl+Shift+N · ⌘⇧N | New session | nothing | no |
  | Ctrl+Shift+E · ⌘⇧E | Terminal sidebar | nothing | no |
  | Ctrl+Shift+S · ⌘⇧S | Session sidebar | nothing | no |
| Ctrl+Shift+Z · ⌘⇧Z | Zen mode | nothing (needs no Shift for ^Z) | no |
  | Ctrl+, · ⌘, | Preferences | nothing | no |
| Escape, Enter, ↑/↓ | the open switcher's | ESC, CR, arrows | only
while a switcher is open |

- **Collisions checked:** Ctrl+Shift+C and Ctrl+Shift+V (copy and paste
in Linux terminals) and Ctrl+Shift+W are not app chords, so they're
untouched.
- **TUIs' own chords:** Claude Code's Shift+Tab mode switch and
Shift+Enter or Alt+Enter new

subject: fix(ci): stop Windows smoke-test processes reliably
body:
Replace native taskkill cleanup with .NET process-tree termination and a bounded exit check. Preserve the ten-second startup assertion and use the same smoke-test code for PR packages and main releases.

The previous main release passed its startup check but failed when the suppressed taskkill command returned exit code 1. Cleanup failures now surface through explicit process operations instead of leaking a native-command exit code.

Validated workflow syntax and formatting, PowerShell process-lifecycle cases, and the PR's platform packaging and smoke tests.

subject: feat(release): ship Linux as an AppImage only, on FUSE 3, with Electron's sandbox (#137)
body:
## What

Linux ships one package: the AppImage, built on the static type2 runtime
so it mounts with FUSE 3 (no libfuse2). The deb and rpm are gone, with
their updaters and CI. `install.sh` installs only the AppImage and,
where AppArmor restricts unprivileged user namespaces (Ubuntu 24.04+),
writes a per-user AppArmor profile once with sudo
(`/etc/apparmor.d/novadeck-appimage-<uid>`, attached to that user's
canonical install and Homebrew paths) so Electron's sandbox starts;
`install.sh --sandbox` writes just the profile. On macOS, `install.sh`
now installs the app too: the universal ZIP, checksum-verified, into
`/Applications` (or `~/Applications` when that is not writable),
replacing the copy already there, refusing while it runs, and holding
interrupts during the swap so a failure never loses the old copy. When
the app runs without the sandbox, a **No sandbox** chip in the footer
explains it and gives the command that fixes it for that install
(`--sandbox`, or the install command for an AppImage elsewhere, or none
when the sandbox was turned off deliberately).

## Why

- deb/rpm updates go through `pkexec` and ask for a password on every
update; the AppImage updates without one.
- On Ubuntu 24.04+ (`kernel.apparmor_restrict_unprivileged_userns=1`)
electron-builder's AppRun probes `unshare -Ur true` and silently adds
`--no-sandbox` when it fails, so AppImage users there ran without a
renderer sandbox and nobody knew. A CI spike (runs 38175671714 →
38175988132) showed GitHub's ubuntu-24.04 runner has the restriction on,
that the release smoke test passed only because of that silent fallback,
and that a profile attached to the AppImage's path restores the sandbox
(renderers in their own user namespace, seccomp on) for the install.sh
path, the `~/.local/bin/novadeck` link and brew's
`~/Applications/novadeck.AppImage`.
- Ubuntu 24.04+ dropped libfuse2, which the old AppImage runtime needed.
- macOS gets the same one-line install. curl leaves the download
unquarantined, so even today's unsigned build opens; it tells of updates
until Developer ID signing lands, after which Squirrel.Mac installs them
in place, as the app stays where this account can replace it.

## Impact

- Linux users get one install path (`curl … install.sh | sh`) and
password-free updates; the password is asked once at install, only where
AppArmor restricts user namespaces.

unsandboxed, and the macOS smoke test installs and

subject: feat(host): update the app from GitHub Releases, with a restart to update (#126)
body:
## What

Novadeck now updates itself from this repo's GitHub Releases. Packaged
builds check about 10 seconds after launch and then every 4 hours, and
download in the background. The update installs on the next quit, and
the footer offers **Update ready · Restart**. Restart saves every page
before the runner stops its shells, the same way quitting does.

| Build | Updates itself |
| --- | --- |
| Linux AppImage | yes |
| Windows NSIS install | yes |
| macOS zip / dmg | only when Developer ID signed; Squirrel.Mac refuses
unsigned apps, so this starts once signing credentials land (#121) |
| deb, rpm, Windows portable, `0.0.0` (PR and local) builds,
`NOVADECK_UPDATES=off` | no |

## Why

There are releases on every merge to main, but a person only gets them
by downloading each one by hand.

## Impact

- **Host** (`application/host/src/main/updater.ts`): electron-updater
6.8.9 with the github provider. `allowPrerelease` is on, because every
release is still a prerelease. A pure `updateMode` decides whether a
build updates itself. The AppImage check needs `execPath` inside
`APPDIR`, so an `APPIMAGE` variable a terminal inherited doesn't count.
The schedule stops once an update has downloaded, because a newer
release found mid-wait would empty the cache the pending install points
at.
- **Restart path:** quitting and restarting share one `shutDown()`. If
`quitAndInstall` fails silently (for example an AppImage in a read-only
folder), a fallback quits after 10 s (30 s on macOS) so the app never
stays open with its shells stopped. On macOS the page hears of an update
only after Squirrel has staged it. A quit caused by OS shutdown or
logoff doesn't install, so the OS can't kill an installer partway
through.
- **Release:** `electron-builder.yml` gets a `publish` entry, so builder
writes `latest*.yml` and blockmaps, and `release.yml` uploads them with
the packages. The AppImage is now `novadeck-linux-x86_64.AppImage` with
no version in the name, so an update keeps the file's path and launchers
keep working.
- **UI:** `onUpdateReady` / `installUpdate` in the protocol bridge,
checked against `updateVersionPattern` on every side. The footer shows
"Update ready · Restart". It never changes the bar's tone, and
connection status keeps its place. A screen reader hears it through a
polite live region. While restarting the button reads "Restarting…", and
at narrow widths only an "Update" button shows. The demo debug panel has
an **Update** group.
- **Docs:** `docs/auto-update
